extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism; practicing journalists; media critics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria that determine what becomes news and how newspapers select, shape, and present information — including economic, procedural, and cognitive constraints. Useful for evaluating newsworthiness, editorial decisions, and institutional biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic dependence on advertisers
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper editor's enterprises depend upon indirect taxation levied by his advertisers upon his readers; the patronage of the advertisers depends upon the editor's skill in holding together an effective group of customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must secure a paying circulation and so select and shape content to attract advertiser-customer groups. This economic motive can bias what is printed and how it is presented: the need to retain a particular audience can trump an abstract notion of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low status and pay for reporting reduces professional standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting, which theoretically constitutes the foundation of the whole institution, is the most poorly paid branch of newspaper work, and is the least regarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because able men often treat straight reporting as temporary, the field lacks corporate traditions (standards of admission, punishment of breaches of the code) that raise professional standards. This underinvestment in reporting talent affects the depth and reliability of news.

rubrics_metrics.name: News requires an overt, objectified act to 'separate itself'
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a manifestation. The course of events must assume a certain definable shape, and until it is in a phase where some aspect is an accomplished fact, news does not separate itself from the ocean of possible truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events become news when they are fixed, objectified, measurable or publicly recorded (e.g., bankruptcy filings, arrests, fires, bills introduced). Rumors or private knowledge typically cannot be published (libel) and are therefore not reported until made overt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited reporters → reliance on standardized routines and watchers
rubrics_metrics.description: All the reporters in the world working all the hours of the day could not witness all the happenings in the world... the range of subjects these comparatively few men manage to cover would be a miracle indeed, if it were not a standardized routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers station watchers at a comparatively small number of places (police HQ, coroner, county clerk, city hall, legislature) and use routines/stereotypes to decide what to cover. This system economizes scarce reporting resources but narrows the kinds of happenings that are noticed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty of news depends on the machinery of record
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a very direct relation between the certainty of news and the system of record. Where there is a good machinery of record, the modern news service works with great precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topics with established, objective recording systems (stock tickers, election counts, vital records, customs) yield reliable, precise news. Weak or absent record systems make reporting uncertain and debatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topics lacking records are debatable or neglected
rubrics_metrics.description: All news about states of mind... descriptions of personalities, sincerity, motive, intention, mass feeling, public opinion... involve data that are at best spasmodically recorded. The news on these subjects is bound to be debatable, when it is not wholly neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects like internal trade, working conditions, unemployment, motives, and national feeling lack stable records or measurements; reporters therefore either report them as opinion/rumor or ignore them unless an overt incident creates a news peg.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press agents/publicity men filter and shape information
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the direct channels to news have been closed and the information for the public is first filtered through publicity agents... they are the media through which news comes. Even statesmen have them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicists select facts and frame situations to present the picture their employers want. Because they answer to employers, not to the public truth, their role introduces bias; journalists relying on press agents will receive pre-shaped accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity often must manufacture news (stunts) to gain attention
rubrics_metrics.description: The good press agent understands that the virtues of his cause are not news... So if the publicity man wishes free publicity he has... to start something. He arranges a stunt: obstructs the traffic, teases the police...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes or organizations seeking coverage may deliberately create overt events to trigger reporting. This explains persistent visibility of groups that can stage incidents and skews news toward spectacle rather than underlying reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource constraints make investigative reporting rare
rubrics_metrics.description: To make plausible a report that conditions are bad, you need a good many columns of print... It is impossible to suppose that any daily newspaper could normally regard the making of Pittsburgh Surveys... as one of its tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In-depth investigations require time, money, and specialized talent; daily newspapers typically lack these resources, so they rarely produce comprehensive exposés of complex social problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: News selection is driven by securing reader attention and identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem of securing attention is by no means equivalent to displaying the news in the perspective laid down by religious teaching or by some form of ethical culture. It is a problem of provoking feeling in the reader, of inducing him to feel a sense of personal identification with the stories he is reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors choose and frame stories to offer readers familiar footholds and stereotypes so they can personally identify with the story quickly. This incentive shapes headlines, placement, and emphasis toward what will absorb the reader’s limited attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stereotypes to cue reader reactions and simplify complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes tell him that if an association of plumbers is called a 'combine' it is appropriate to develop his hostility; if it is called a 'group of leading business men' the cue is for a favorable reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stereotyped labels and conventional frames help readers integrate news quickly but also channel their feelings and predispose interpretations, enabling media to create opinion through selection and wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors favor indisputable facts and easy interest under deadline pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Every bulletin requires a swift but complicated judgment... Without standardization... the editor would soon die of excitement... The indisputable fact and the easy interest, are the strike itself and the reader's inconvenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competition, deadlines, libel risk, and fixed page space push editors to simplify, prioritize immediate, indisputable events and to avoid subtle or unconventional angles that take more space and risk alienating readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: News often reports overt phases rather than root causes (e.g., strikes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The underlying trouble appears in the news through certain easily recognizable symptoms, a demand, a strike, disorder... The bulletins from the scene of action will note the trouble that arose from the assertion, rather than the reasons which led to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage of disputes typically emphasizes stoppages, disorder, and reader inconvenience rather than the complex antecedent conditions (working environment, standards of living). This skews public perception away from systemic causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorials and interpretive clues integrate news and guide reader opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials reinforce. Sometimes in a situation that on the news pages is too confusing to permit of identification, they give the reader a clue by means of which he engages himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial pages often provide the interpretive framework readers use to make sense of confusing news. This coupling of news and editorial comment amplifies the paper's ability to shape public opinion and stabilize reader identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty reporting chaotic or censored events leads to stereotype-driven coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The hardest thing to report is chaos... This put the formulating of Russian news at its source... into the hands of censors and propagandists. They were for a long time subject to no check of any kind... created... a set of stereotypes so evocative of hate and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When access is closed (war censorship, language barriers) reporting is dominated by correspondents/censors outside the scene or by propagandists; news becomes constructed through stereotypes and can misrepresent the reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-newspaper influence shapes reporting techniques and models
rubrics_metrics.description: When the war broke out... certain dailies, rich enough to pay cable tolls, took the lead in securing news, and the way that news was presented became a model for the whole press... It came from the English press... because it was easier to buy English correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers imitate styles and frames developed by better-resourced outlets; reliance on a few dominant sources or foreign centers concentrates particular reporting technics and perspectives across the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivated reader partisanship makes papers reluctant to change positions
rubrics_metrics.description: The more passionately involved he becomes, the more he will tend to resent not only a different view... That is why many a newspaper finds that, having honestly evoked the partisanship of its readers, it can not easily... change position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once an editor has built an engaged, partially partisan readership, switching editorial stance risks losing audience and is managed with difficulty; papers may let coverage taper off instead of revising opinion, leading to entrenched biases.
